source: Tejani et al., Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM): 2024 Update, Radiology: Artificial Intelligence 2024, doi 10.1148/ryai.240300; the short item texts as its checklist table gives them

items.asks: Identification as a study of AI methodology, specifying the category of technology used (eg, deep learning)
items.evidence: Measuring the gap between synthetic and real X-rays with deep convolutional features and two-sample tests: a pre-registered comparison of digitally reconstructed radiographs made by FleXray's recipe, and of its FluXray edits, with real fluoroscopy and plain film, and a replication test of the recipe's renderer.

items.asks: Summary of study design, methods, results, and conclusions
items.evidence: In a pre-registered study of existing images, 10,127 images in 21 groups (11 synthetic, 3 fluoroscopy, 7 plain film; 20 groups tested, the one-person hip phantom plotted only) were decoded one way and embedded in FleXray's own encoder and an ImageNet ResNet-18, read inversion-invariant. Groups were compared by person-grouped classifier two-sample tests (logistic AUC with a person-cluster bootstrap interval and a permutation p), the unbiased MMD with person-level permutations and Benjamini-Hochberg q, FD64 and PRDC, calibrated by split-half nulls and real-against-real baselines. Each of the seven synthetic sets whose family contrasts the summary prints was told apart from real fluoroscopy and from film. For the primary endpoints, against fluoroscopy and then film: this project's render of FleXray's recipe with the attenuation randomisation off gave AUC 0.94 [0.89, 0.98] and 0.96 [0.94, 0.98]; the same physics from the CT alone gave 0.89 [0.83, 0.94] and 0.93 [0.90, 0.96]; FluXray gave 1.00 [0.99, 1.00] and 0.95 [0.94, 0.96]. The split-half nulls flagged nothing (median AUC 0.49 in FleXray's space). No primary endpoint read "indistinguishable". Every one read "closer than two real corpora", a word at its ceiling here, because two real corpora were told apart at least as surely (median AUC 1.00, least 0.97, over 36 pairs). Rendering the same recipe through this project's blocks and through FleXray's own code read "not replicated": MMD q 0.046 (0.043 without the nulls) with an AUC of 0.50 [0.50, 0.50]. That word rests on the MMD alone, its q 0.004 under the bar and within the permutations' Monte Carlo margin, and under it every comparison through the blocks is of this project's renders, not FleXray's.

items.asks: Scientific and/or clinical background, including the intended use and role of the AI approach
items.evidence: SchwingNet names vertebral levels on intraoperative fluoroscopy. There, real frames exist but their level labels are the cost, so DRRs rendered from CT are a candidate source of training data. In the record, a detector trained on renders alone found 71.67 percent of vertebral bodies on real film. One trained on film found 97.6, 99.14 or 99.2 percent: three readings of the same three misses in 243 that the record has not settled. FleXray is a segmenter trained on CT-projected labels and FluXray's FLUX.2-edited renders, with real radiographs only of the limbs (arXiv 2609.26756v2). Given C-ArmLSpine's truth boxes, it named 99.14 percent of them. It is zero-shot on those frames by its configs, though not yet confirmed by file (audit item 6). This study measures how far such synthetic images lie from real fluoroscopy and film, compared with the distance between two real corpora. It also asks whether this project's render blocks reproduce FleXray's own renders. It informs the FleXray audit (#391, items 6 to 11). Its AI is an instrument: frozen pretrained encoders and two-sample classifiers that measure a distribution gap. No model is built for any clinical use.

the question, PREREG.md section 1: how far FleXray's synthetic DRRs are from real X-rays, plain film and intra-operative fluoroscopy, whether that distance is larger than the distance between two real corpora, and whether this project's rendering of FleXray's recipe reproduces FleXray's own; the hypotheses and their bars, its section 4: the primary endpoints, in the flexray space read inversion-invariant, the logistic C2ST AUC of flexray_drr, of flexray_drr_ct and of fluxray where fetched against pooled fluoroscopy and against pooled film, each with its interval, and FD64 of each against each family divided by the median FD64 between that family's own real corpora, the gap ratio, 1 meaning as far as two real corpora are from each other; the words beside each primary number, indistinguishable where the AUC's lower bound is at most 0.6, closer than two real corpora where it is below the median AUC of the family's real pairs and separable otherwise; and the replication, replicated for each of the two worded pairs, flexray_replica against flexray_reference and fluxray_raw against fluxray_raw_reference, where the logistic AUC's lower bound is at most 0.6 and the MMD's q at least 0.05, and not replicated otherwise, the first pair's word in that space and reading being the study's verdict

Retrospective: no person was imaged or enrolled for this study. The real groups are image corpora the project already held, which the sample index lists (PREREG.md section 2); the seven render groups are rendered in the job from held CTs; and the other synthetic groups are sets made before the study, FluXray's from the FleXray data fetched on 2026-10-26. The analysis was pre-registered: PREREG.md froze it on 2026-10-27, before any number of the study was read (its section 7).

a measurement under pre-registered hypotheses: the primary endpoints and the replication verdict of PREREG.md section 4, every other number read as description (its section 6); the study trains no network and builds no model for use

The render groups' images were made in the job from 26 held TotalSegmentator v2.0.1 CTs (27 chosen, 26 kept by every group) by FleXray's released MOOSE recipe, through this project's render blocks or FleXray's own code, each group changing the blocks the groups table names: flexray_drr (MOOSE labels, attenuation randomisation off), flexray_drr_ct (no labels, FleXray's axial crops drawn uniformly, each aimed at its own centre, attenuation off), flexray_replica (MOOSE labels) and flexray_reference (the same through FleXray's own code), flexray_spineps (SPINEPS labels), and fluxray_raw and fluxray_raw_reference (the paper's raw recipe: whole volume, FluXray's pose grid, cone projection, attenuation off, min-max scaling, 4 views at 1,024 pixels, through the blocks and through FleXray's code). FluXray's images were made by its authors: by the paper (README section 2.3), FLUX.2 klein 9B edited each raw render (4 steps, bfloat16, guidance 1), pixels whose raw DRR was below 0.05 were set to 0, a paired-difference filter dropped about 4 percent of the edits per pose, and the release resized the 1,024-pixel edits to 512, where the project's notes record the stored images at 256. The other synthetic sets are the project's own earlier renders and styled images. The real corpora were acquired by their publishers under their own protocols, which this study does not record beyond what it notes of them: C-ArmLSpine's AP and lateral spot frames of one mobile C-arm, narrow and centred on the lumbar spine; DeepFluoro's vendor fluoroscopy of cadaver pelves, six specimens and two phantoms; a resin hip phantom's fluoroscopy; and plain films (lumbar, whole-spine, cervical, abdominal and cephalometric) from their releases, as JPEG re-exports, 16-bit scans or DICOM.

items.asks: Implications for practice, including intended use and/or clinical role
items.evidence: The study has no clinical role and supports no diagnostic use. It is a measurement that informs the FleXray audit's items 6 to 11. On the record, none of the seven synthetic sets whose family contrasts the summary prints is indistinguishable from real fluoroscopy or film in these feature spaces. Those seven include this project's renders of FleXray's recipe and FluXray's released FLUX-edited images, so none passes for real frames by this test. Because the replication read "not replicated", every comparison made through this project's render blocks is of this project's renders, not FleXray's (PREREG.md section 5). Separability alone does not predict that a network trained on such images fails on real frames. FleXray, trained with no real spine frame by its configs, named 99.14 percent of C-ArmLSpine's truth boxes when given the boxes.

items.asks: Statement about the availability of software, trained model, and/or data
items.evidence: No model was trained, so none is released. The code and the study's records are in a private repository and are confidential; nothing of them goes public before the provisional patent is filed. The code is tools/domain_gap.py, tools/domain_gap_stats.py, tools/flexray_render.py, tools/render_blocks.py, and src/schwingnet/domain_gap.py, render_blocks.py and segmenters.py. results.json, the figures and the plan stay on Wayne State's grid; only BENCH.md and summary.txt left it. The real images and FluXray are third-party corpora under their own terms, several non-commercial or held by agreement: DeepFluoro and FluXray under CC BY-NC 4.0, BUU-LSPINE under its end-user agreement, AASCE by request form, and IEEE DataPort's set by subscription. They are not redistributed and are available from their publishers. The project's own synthetic sets and renders stay on the grid.
